sections.title: Why Skin Disease Burden Is Hard to Measure
sections.markdown:
Skin conditions can cause pain, disfigurement, disability and stigma, and they carry psychological, social and financial costs. Researchers and doctors usually measure this burden with questionnaires that patients fill in themselves. The authors argue that these questionnaires probably underestimate how much skin disease affects people's lives. To test that, they reviewed every questionnaire designed for use across skin conditions in general and graded how well each had been tested.

## Why measurement matters in dermatology

A **patient-reported outcome measure (PROM)** is a standard questionnaire that records the patient's own account of their health, symptoms or quality of life (QoL). These tools carry extra weight in dermatology because treatment often aims to make life better rather than longer.

The authors' earlier interview research with patients produced a framework that defines "impact" across five areas: physical, psychological, social, financial and daily functioning. Measured against that framework, existing QoL questionnaires have four weaknesses:

- They are designed to test whether a treatment improves a patient's life. How much the skin condition itself affects that life is a different question.
- They leave out areas that matter. Psychological items focus on emotions and, to a lesser degree, coping, and mostly ignore cognition, meaning what people believe about their illness. In psoriasis, those beliefs predict outcomes better than a clinician's rating of severity, and they are closely linked to whether patients take their medication.
- Skin conditions do damage that builds up over the years, which the field calls **cumulative life course impairment** (it can shape major life decisions, for example). Current questionnaires have no items that could track this over time.
- Most have never been assessed against COSMIN, the accepted standard for judging health questionnaires.

That last point matters because a questionnaire only produces meaningful numbers if it meets set criteria for validity (does it measure what it claims to?), reliability (does it give consistent answers?) and responsiveness (does the score move when the patient's condition changes?). Without that evidence, nobody can say how far to trust its data.

This review is the first step toward a new tool, the Patient-Reported Impact of Dermatological Diseases (PRIDD) measure, meant for adults worldwide in research and clinical practice. It had three aims: find every dermatology-specific PROM and judge whether any could measure impact, rate their measurement properties, and make evidence-based recommendations.

sections.title: How the Review Worked
sections.markdown:
The team registered its plan in advance on PROSPERO (CRD42018108829), a public registry of systematic review protocols, which makes it harder to change methods after seeing results. They searched PubMed, PsycInfo and CINAHL from the start of each database to 25 June 2018. The search combined three groups of terms: skin conditions, life impact, and a validated filter for finding studies of measurement properties. There was no language limit, and non-English papers were translated. Questionnaires built for a single disease, such as atopic dermatitis, turned up in such numbers that they will be reported in a separate paper.

Three reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then ranked the full articles. Each checked 10% of another reviewer's work, and they settled disagreements by discussion.

The appraisal followed the **COSMIN** method (Consensus-based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments), which works on two levels. First, six reviewers used a risk-of-bias checklist to rate how well each study was designed and run. Second, they rated the result for each measurement property against preset thresholds as sufficient, insufficient, indeterminate or inconsistent. They did not assess criterion validity, which compares a tool against a gold standard, because no gold standard exists for something like quality of life.

The two ratings were then pooled for each property of each questionnaire, and the evidence was graded high, moderate, low or very low using a modified form of GRADE, a common evidence-rating system. Standard GRADE lowers the grade for five reasons. COSMIN drops publication bias, since no registries exist for measurement studies, and keeps the other four: risk of bias, inconsistent results, indirectness (evidence from a different population or setting) and imprecision. Each language version of a questionnaire counted as a separate instrument.

Each questionnaire was then placed in one of three categories that work like a traffic light:

- Category A (green): ready to use without further validation.
- Category B (amber): can be recommended, but needs more validation.
- Category C (red): not recommended.

sections.title: What They Found
sections.markdown:
The search returned 12,925 abstracts, and 3 more articles came from reference lists and expert input. In the end, 36 questionnaires described in 46 articles went into the COSMIN analysis.

None of them measures full impact. Most (83%) measured QoL. The areas they covered most often were symptoms, emotional or psychological functioning, physical functioning, social functioning and daily activities. None covered financial impact or life course impairment, so none should be treated as a complete measure of what living with a skin disease involves.

Patients also had little say in how the tools were built. The authors treat **content validity** as the most important property: whether the questions cover what matters to patients, which can only be established by asking patients. For almost every questionnaire the only evidence came from development and pilot studies (22 in total), and 86% of those were of very low methodological quality. Only the Spanish version of Skindex-29 had a dedicated content validity study. Three questionnaires had development work of adequate quality: the Patient Benefit Index (PBI), the Turkish Quality of Life instrument (TQL) and Spanish Skindex-29. The most common reason for a very low grade was that cognitive interviews, where patients talk through how they understand each question, were either skipped or done poorly.

Testing was patchy. No questionnaire had been tested on every property, and each had between 1 and 6 properties tested. Internal consistency (whether the items on a scale hang together) was tested most often, 37 times. Measurement invariance was tested twice, and measurement error was never tested.

The final recommendations:

- Category A: none.
- Category B: 31 questionnaires.
- Category C: 5, each with high-quality evidence of insufficient properties. These were the Sinhala version of the Dermatology Life Quality Index, the short form of the Questionnaire on Experience with Skin Complaints, the Serbian and Spanish versions of Skindex-29, and the Chinese version of Skindex-16.

The discussion section gives slightly different counts (30 and 6).

When no tool reaches category A, COSMIN advises provisionally recommending the category B tool with the best evidence for content validity. On that basis the PBI is provisionally recommended for measuring patient needs and treatment benefits, and the TQL for QoL. Both come with a caveat: their content validity studies were of acceptable quality, but the results were inconsistent.

The paper also profiles several well-known tools:

- **Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI):** the most familiar of these tools. It had high-quality evidence of sufficient internal consistency, construct validity and responsiveness, but its reliability evidence was indeterminate. One study found a ceiling effect, with 11% of patients at the top of the scale. Reported thresholds for its minimally important difference (the smallest change in score that patients find meaningful) ranged from 2.34 to 5.7.
- **Dermatology-specific Quality of Life:** showed floor effects, with many patients at the lowest possible score on some subscales (41.2% and 53.8% on work/school in two studies).
- **FLQA-d:** a version of the Freiburg Life Quality Assessment for long-term skin conditions. It had high-quality evidence of insufficient internal consistency.
- **Skindex family:** the original Skindex had indeterminate structural validity and weak evidence for construct validity. Its revisions, Skindex-29 and Skindex-16, did better on several properties.

sections.title: Why It Matters, and the Review's Strengths and Limits
sections.markdown:
The authors say that using questionnaires of poor or unknown quality is wasteful and unethical, because invalid or unreliable tools can produce misleading results. That applies both to clinical trials and to treatment decisions for individual patients. An imperfect tool may still be better than none, but users should know its limits and temper their conclusions accordingly. The findings agree with an earlier COSMIN review of QoL instruments used in eczema.

Translations are a particular concern. Four of the five red-category questionnaires were translations. No translated version in any category had been tested for **measurement invariance**, which checks that a translated item measures the same thing in the same way as the original. Without that check, results from different language versions cannot be pooled or compared. The authors call for standard methods in translation studies (such as forward- and back-translation) and a standard set of properties to test.

## Strengths and limits

Because nothing passed, some might argue COSMIN is too strict. The authors respond that experts from many disciplines built it, and another review team judged it more lenient than the older OMERACT approach. It reduces bias and allows standard comparisons between tools. It also has flaws: it treats poor reporting the same as poor methods, and it does a weak job of assessing studies that use Rasch analysis, a statistical approach the authors consider better than classical test theory. The review did not search the reference lists of included studies, which may explain why some translations were missed. At least three reviewers worked at each stage, and two of them took part in every step to keep judgments consistent.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Case for a New Measure
sections.markdown: Under COSMIN standards, no dermatology-specific questionnaire can be recommended without reservation. The most common reason is that patients had too little input when the tools were first built. No existing tool measures the impact of skin disease across conditions, so the authors argue for PRIDD, a new measure developed with substantial patient input.

anchors.quote: We believe there is a need to standardize cross-cultural translation studies of PROMs in terms of methods (e.g. back- and forward-translation procedures) and measurement properties tested.

anchors.sentence: Because nothing passed, some might argue COSMIN is too strict.
The authors respond that experts from many disciplines built it, and another review team judged it more lenient than the older OMERACT approach.
It reduces bias and allows standard comparisons between tools.
anchors.quote: Use of COSMIN is a strength of this review as it: (i) reduces bias in the evaluation of measurement properties; (ii) allows comparisons between PROMs; (iii) enables standardized recommendations; and (iv) highlights issues in the field, including poor methodological quality and reporting.

anchors.sentence: It also has flaws: it treats poor reporting the same as poor methods, and it does a weak job of assessing studies that use Rasch analysis, a statistical approach the authors consider better than classical test theory.
anchors.quote: In addition, COSMIN tools do not adequately evaluate the methodological quality of studies conducted with Rasch analysis, which is considered superior to the CTT framework, since they make limited reference to Rasch relevant statistics.

anchors.sentence: The review did not search the reference lists of included studies, which may explain why some translations were missed.
anchors.quote: However, reference lists of included studies were not searched, which may explain why some translated PROMs were not found.

anchors.sentence: At least three reviewers worked at each stage, and two of them took part in every step to keep judgments consistent.
anchors.quote: Finally, at least 3 independent reviewers were involved in screening, data extraction and analysis; 2 of whom were involved at every step to ensure consistency.

anchors.sentence: Under COSMIN standards, no dermatology-specific questionnaire can be recommended without reservation.
anchors.quote: This study found that no dermatology-specific PROMs could be unreservedly recommended for use according to the COSMIN standards.

anchors.sentence: The most common reason is that patients had too little input when the tools were first built.
anchors.quote: The single most common reason for poor quality assessment was the lack of patient input to the initial development of the measure.

anchors.sentence: No existing tool measures the impact of skin disease across conditions, so the authors argue for PRIDD, a new measure developed with substantial patient input.
anchors.quote: No measure of impact across skin conditions exists in dermatology and, therefore, we argue that the new measure PRIDD, developed with substantial patient input, is warranted.

sources.abstract: By relying on data from existing patient-reported outcome measures of quality of life, the true impact of skin conditions on patients’ lives may be underestimated. This study systematically reviewed all dermatology-specific (used across skin conditions) patient-reported outcome measures and makes evidence-based recommendations for their use. The study protocol is registered on PROSPERO (CRD42018108829). PubMed, PsycInfo and CINAHL were searched from inception to 25 June 2018. The Consensus-based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) criteria were used to assess the measurement properties and methodological quality of studies. A total of 12,925 abstracts were identified. Zero patient-reported outcome measures were assigned to category A (ready for use without further validation), 31 to category B (recommended for use, but only with further validation) and 5 to category C (not recommended for use). There is no gold-standard dermatology-specific patient-reported outcome measure that can be recommended or used without caution. A new measure that can comprehensively capture the impact of dermatological conditions on the patient’s life is needed.
sources.sec2/p1: The search identified 12,925 abstracts. An additional 3 articles (–) were identified through reference lists and expert input. details the full article selection process. Of the 53 dermatology-specific PROM articles identified, data were extracted from 52 articles. One article () was excluded, since the psychometric testing for 2 separate PROMs was combined. Two studies examined more than one PROM (, ). Six articles that met inclusion criteria were not included in the COSMIN analysis, but data were extracted (, –); 2 because only interpretability information was reported (, ); and 4 review articles did not provide sufficient information on the methodological quality of included studies, but included information on interpretability and feasibility (, , , ). In all, 36 PROMs (Tables SII and SIII), reported in 46 articles (Table SIV), were included in the COSMIN analysis.
sources.sec2.2/p1: shows the methodological quality of studies and the quality of the results for the PROM content validity studies. Evidence for content validity was based only on development and pilot-testing studies (n = 22) for most instruments, as a content validity study was conducted only for the Spanish version of Skindex-29 (S29-S). The majority (86%) of the development studies were of very low methodological quality. Only the Patient Benefit Index (PBI; low quality), Turkish Quality of Life Instrument (TQL; low quality) and Skindex 29-Spanish (high quality) were rated as having adequate methodological quality. The most common reason for the downgrading of the overall quality of evidence to very low was that a cognitive interview was not conducted or was of poor methodological quality.
sources.sec2.2/p2: The methodological quality of studies on measurement properties () and quality of the measurement properties () per study are also presented. No PROM was tested for all measurement properties. The amount of measurement properties tested per PROM ranged between 1 and 6. Internal consistency was the most popular psychometric test (n = 37), measurement invariance the least (n = 2) and measurement error was not tested at all.
sources.sec2.1/p1: A comparison of each PROM at the domain level is shown in . Domains were derived based on the subscales reported by the developers or through structural validity analyses (i.e. factor analysis). Many of the instruments (83%) measured QoL. The most common domains observed were symptoms, emotional/psychological functioning, physical functioning, social functioning and daily activities. None of the PROMs included other life domains, such as financial impact and life course impairment; therefore, they should not be considered a comprehensive measure of the impact of living with a skin disease.
sources.sec3/p1: To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically evaluate published dermatology-specific PROMs in accordance with the COSMIN guidelines. A total of 36 dermatology-specific PROMs were identified and the majority measured QoL. Examination of the instruments at the domain level revealed that no single PROM could comprehensively assess the impact of living with a skin condition according to our conceptual framework, indicating that the development of a new PRIDD measure is warranted.
sources.sec1/p2: The systematic review was conducted according to the COSMIN methodology which is the gold-standard critical appraisal tool for systematic reviews of PROMs (). According to COSMIN, all PROMs in a review should be assessed according to both the construct of interest and target population of the review (). The aim of this review was to identify measures of impact and to establish the quality of dermatology-specific PROMs currently in use. As such, the target population was patients with dermatological conditions (as opposed to disease-specific samples, e.g. atopic dermatitis) and the construct of interest was that of the PROM assessed. This allowed us to both identify measures of impact and establish the quality of PROMs currently used in dermatology.
sources.sec3/p4: Four of the 5 PROMs not recommended for use were translated versions of other PROMs, potentially indicating an issue with current practise in cross-cultural translation. Our findings cannot generalize to all translated PROMs in dermatology, as we did not find published development and validation studies for some known translations. It does seem, however, that there are issues in the translation of PROMs in this area. There was a lack of measurement invariance (or cross-cultural validity) testing for translated PROMs in any recommendation category. Measurement invariance is core to the process of validation as it provides evidence of “construct equivalence”, the assumption that items in the translated version measure the same construct in the same way as in the original version (–). Evidence of construct equivalence, therefore, is required to synthesize and compare data across the language versions with obvious implications for research. We believe there is a need to standardize cross-cultural translation studies of PROMs in terms of methods (e.g. back- and forward-translation procedures) and measurement properties tested.
